title: Evacuate the Doomed Base — Retreat East to the Safe Zone

raw.realWorldMeaning: The primary base is being overrun by a heavy assault that structurally cannot be repelled with the units on hand — the fact and proc WILL fall regardless of what the agent does. The correct play is not to fight the doomed-defence (sunk cost) but to EVACUATE the remaining mobile force EAST to a pre-designated safe zone before attrition reduces the column below the survival floor. Win = ≥3 of the 5 starting tanks inside the safe-zone radius, ≥3 still alive, before the deadline. Stalling loses (the assault wipes the immobile tanks at the base); holding loses (the heavy + rocket composition out-trades the 2tnk column); only the prompt EVAC-east order wins.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Business-Continuity-Planning (BCP) evacuation and NFPA / FEMA emergency-management EVAC doctrine — when shelter-in-place is no longer survivable, the policy must abandon the compromised site and route to the pre-designated muster point. Same pattern in cloud-incident response (drain a region under irrecoverable outage to a healthy peer), in wildfire and chemical-spill EVAC, and in SC2 GG-walk macro micro (preserve the army when the base cannot be saved).
raw.benchmarkAnchor: BCP evacuation (business continuity planning), emergency management EVAC (NFPA / FEMA muster-point doctrine), SC2 retreat / GG-walk: preserve army when base is doomed, cloud incident region-drain to healthy peer

title: Defense in Depth — Two Bands Beat One Thick Wall

raw.realWorldMeaning: A heavy enemy wave drives straight at your construction yard. The same finite pillbox budget massed into ONE thick wall has no depth: when the wave punches a hole, the survivors sail through the breach and raze the base. The SAME pillboxes split into a FRONT line (which absorbs and thins the first impact) plus a REAR line at greater depth (which shreds the survivors that break through) contains the breach instead of suffering it. title: Defense in Depth — Two Layers, Not One Thick Wall

raw.realWorldMeaning: Defense-in-depth doctrine: against a massed concentrated rush, a front line plus a second line at greater depth shreds the attacker after the first layer falls, where a single fortified line — even one with the same brick count — eventually collapses under sustained pressure and razes the base behind it. Picking concentration vs distribution is the reasoning load: the same four pillboxes massed in one cluster lose, the same four pillboxes spread thin in one long line lose, and only a 2+2 layered topology survives.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Multi-layer security architecture (defense-in-depth): a single perimeter firewall, however thick, eventually gets breached; the same defensive capacity deployed as outer + inner layers (each covering the same arc) absorbs the breach. Same total resources, different topology, qualitatively different survivability. Also: medieval keep + outer-wall design (attackers must take BOTH); redundant systems architecture (one component failure ≠ system failure).

title: Distributed Defense — Split Across Concurrent Lanes

raw.realWorldMeaning: Enemy waves attack the centrally-placed base concurrently from multiple cardinal directions. Distributing defenders evenly across each active lane holds every approach; concentrating on one lane leaves the other lanes uncontested — those waves stride untouched to the construction yard and raze it. This is the canonical multi-front / graph min-cut allocation problem: defensive capacity must be matched to the cardinality of concurrent threats, not to the loudest single threat.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Distributed-systems load balancing under N concurrent request streams: each stream needs at least one worker, or its queue builds without bound and the SLA breaks regardless of how well the other streams are served. Likewise air-defence sector coverage: pooling all batteries in one sector leaves the others open. Same total capacity, different topology, qualitatively different system survivability.

title: Fortify the Threat Axis — Pre-Position Defence on the Intel Lane

raw.realWorldMeaning: Spatial commitment of a finite defence budget to the CORRECT direction given declared intel. The mission brief states where the enemy will attack from; the agent must invest its pillboxes on that lane (and not the opposite lane). A correct-axis commitment blunts the rush; a wrong-axis commitment lets the rushers walk past and the run loses on the spatial clause. This is the decision drill of pre-positioned defence: not "should I defend?" but "WHERE should I defend, given what intel says?".
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Intel-driven facility hardening: a security operator is told the threat axis (a perimeter breach is expected on the EAST gate) and must commit the available barriers / sensors / responders to that axis. Spending the same budget on the WEST gate satisfies no objective. This pack tests whether the policy converts a textual directional cue into a CORRECT spatial commitment.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: ERQA spatial commit, MicroRTS terrain-aware defense, military pre-positioned defense, intel-driven facility hardening

title: Scout the Axis, Then Fortify — Intel-Driven Adaptive Defense

raw.realWorldMeaning: Adaptive defense under uncertainty: the threat axis is NOT known a priori; the agent must drive its scouts to discover the enemy's forward outpost (where the build-up actually is), then commit pillboxes on THAT lane, then engage. Pre-committing to a single direction without scouting is the classical Maginot-Line failure mode — defenses on the wrong axis are dead weight while the unguarded lane is overrun. The capability under test is the intel-action loop: observation FIRST, commitment SECOND.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Intel-driven facility hardening / military reactive defense: a perimeter operator does not know which gate will be breached; they must dispatch reconnaissance, confirm the threat axis from sensor returns, and then deploy barriers / responders on the confirmed lane. Skipping the reconnaissance step and pre-staging on a guessed lane is correct half the time and catastrophically wrong the other half. The robust doctrine is scout-then-fortify, not commit-on-faith.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: PlanBench replanning, military reactive defense, intel-driven defense
raw.author: openra-bench

title: Central Reserve — Stage Mobile Force at Centre, Move Out to Intercept

raw.realWorldMeaning: A rush is incoming, but the flank it will arrive from is uncertain at decision time. A small mobile armoured reserve is pre-staged at the centre of the engagement zone — equidistant from both candidate flanks. The reserve MUST move OUT of the centre toward the localised threat lane(s) to intercept the rush before it reaches the construction yard. Pre-committing to one flank wins only when the rush arrives on that flank and LOSES otherwise (the reserve cannot pivot back in time); holding passively at the centre lets the auto-engagement kill some attackers but satisfies no forward-zone objective. The canonical answer is centralisation + forward commitment — military "general reserve" / chess centralization doctrine.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Quick-reaction force / on-call incident responder: the responder is stationed at a hub equidistant from candidate incident sites, not committed to any one site in advance. When an alert localises the incident, the responder DEPLOYS FORWARD to that site — staying at the hub or committing in advance to the wrong site both fail the response SLA.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: military reserve doctrine (central reserve responds to any flank), chess-piece centralization principle, rapid-response force doctrine, MicroRTS reactive defense from centre
raw.author: openra-bench

title: Reactive Defense — Reinforce the Breached Lane

raw.realWorldMeaning: A multi-lane defence with a mobile armoured reserve held uncommitted at the centre. At first both lanes face only a light probe, but mid-episode one lane is BREACHED by a heavier wave. The light garrison there cannot hold the breach alone; the agent must react — read which lane was breached — and shift the mobile reserve FORWARD into that lane to reinforce it before the line collapses. Holding the reserve at the centre, or committing it to the quiet lane, lets the breach overrun the line. The pack tests reactive reserve commitment: identify the developing breach and commit the reserve to the sector that is actually being hit.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Incident surge response: an on-call response team is staged centrally, equidistant from candidate sites. When one site escalates into a breach, the surge capacity must be committed to THAT site — promptly and in force. Holding the reserve back or dispatching it to a quiet site both fail the response: the skill is reading where the main effort has localised and committing the reserve there.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: military reserve commitment, reinforce the breach doctrine, incident surge response
raw.author: openra-bench

title: Strategic Withdrawal — Retreat from the Forward Base and Rebuild at Depth

raw.realWorldMeaning: The forward base is being overrun by a heavy attack that cannot be repulsed inside the tick / cash budget; the right move is to ACCEPT THE LOSS of the forward position, fall back to a deeper safe zone (pre-staged with an MCV and a power plant), DEPLOY the MCV to spawn a new Construction Yard there, and BUILD a refinery so production stands up at depth. Trying to hold the forward base bleeds the defenders and the deadline expires with neither base alive. Stalling, hold-forward, or deploy-only-no-rebuild all lose: only the recognise-and-withdraw policy reconstitutes a live fact + proc post-retreat.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Business-continuity failover and military strategic withdrawal: the primary production site is being lost and heroic defence is infeasible; standing up the cold-standby site (DR site, backup datacentre, fall-back command post) BEFORE the primary fully falls is the goal, not preserving the primary. title: Ambush Trigger Discipline — Lift Stance to Engage the Inbound Rush

raw.realWorldMeaning: A defended-overwatch / ambush trigger drill: four medium tanks are pre-staged at a choke between the inbound enemy column and the construction yard. Their standing orders are HoldFire (stance:0) — they will not fire on their own. The mission is to call `set_stance` to lift the engagement authority so all four tanks auto-engage the rush at cannon range and wipe it before it reaches the base. Never flipping the stance leaves the position functionally undefended (the rush walks through unopposed and razes the base); the controllable verb that turns the pre-staged position into an active defence is the stance flip.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: A weapon-system safety interlock: a turret / drone-swarm perimeter is pre-staged and aimed at the avenue of approach, but the trigger authority is held by the operator. The operator MUST issue the engagement-authority command for the system to fire on the inbound target; without that command the perimeter is functionally a passive observation post and the target reaches the protected asset. The skill is the operator's decision to LIFT the engagement-authority lock at all — not the precise moment within the engagement window.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: military rules-of-engagement (ROE) ambush doctrine, SC2 stance micro — hold-then-attack siege-tank salvo, ambush doctrine — engagement authority lifted on trigger
raw.author: openra-bench

title: Surprise Flank — Intel Said North, Enemy Came South: Detect and Redeploy

raw.realWorldMeaning: The mission brief states the enemy will attack from the NORTH and the terrain reinforces it: a rocky band on the north edge forms a natural chokepoint, with two pillboxes pre-built to cover it. The four pre-placed defenders are distributed around the construction yard — not yet committed to either lane. MID-EPISODE a rusher band actually arrives from the SOUTH (the open flank) via a scheduled spawn. The decision is whether the agent trusts the announced direction + terrain cue and watches its construction yard get razed, or detects the actual attack axis from the spawn event, leaves the wrong-axis pillboxes silent, and commits the defenders SOUTH to intercept the real rush before it reaches the fact.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Misdirection-aware defence / military adversarial robustness on a directional axis: a fortified flank that the enemy has bypassed must be ABANDONED in favour of the actual contact axis, even though doing so contradicts the announced plan and "wastes" the pre-built fortification. The classical failure mode this trains against is "fighting the plan, not the enemy": the operator sticks to the announced threat axis even after the ground-truth signal contradicts it. Robust security operations require that the response policy treat announced threat intelligence as a PRIOR, not a guarantee, and commit to the observed axis when the two diverge.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: adversarial robustness / surprise-axis reaction, opponent-modeling: detect deception, military reactive defense / flank discipline, CICERO deception handling
raw.author: openra-bench

title: Defense Topology — Match Towers to Threat Geometry (Line or Cluster)

raw.realWorldMeaning: Defensive structure placement is geometry-sensitive: a wide-front attack across many rows demands a LINE that covers each row; a concentrated thrust through one chokepoint demands a CLUSTER of overlapping fire at the choke. Both topologies waste budget on the wrong geometry — a cluster against a spread attack leaves the flanks open; a line against a funnel under-defends the choke. The capability is reading the attacker's forcing geometry from the map and the threat composition, then committing the defense topology that matches.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Firewall / WAF rule placement. When traffic enters across many paths (broad ingress, microservices), the right architecture is a rule per path — a layered spread. When all traffic MUST traverse a single ingress (one API gateway, one bridge), the right architecture is dense layered inspection AT that point. A defender who deploys the wrong topology for the wrong threat surface either overspends on one path and leaves others open, or under-protects the actual ingress.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: graph theory min-cut (concentrate defenses at chokepoints), military bunker placement doctrine, firewall topology: dense at chokepoints, perimeter doctrine (cover the full approach width), Lanchester defense concentration
raw.author: openra-bench

en:
Four rifle squads (3 each) advance west on four separate rows — y=4, 12, 28, 36 — each toward its own decoy on the same row at x=4. Budget $2400 buys four pillboxes. Place one on each of the four attacker rows at x=60 so every squad walks into a pillbox's range. Clustering all four at the centre (y=20) leaves every row out of weapon range; the cluster kills nothing and the squads raze your yard. Yard intact, eight kills, within about 60 turns.
WIN WHEN: own ≥4 'pbox' building(s) AND have 1 building(s) near (60,4) AND have 1 building(s) near (60,12) AND have 1 building(s) near (60,28) AND have 1 building(s) near (60,36) AND destroy ≥8 enemy units AND own ≥1 'fact' building(s) AND before game tick 5400.
YOU LOSE IF: (not before game tick 5401 OR NOT (own ≥1 'fact' building(s))).
You have at most 60 decision turns; acting decisively and early matters.

A single 5-cell corridor at x=60, y=18..22 is the only way west. Ten attackers (eight rifles + two rocket soldiers) must funnel through it to reach your construction yard at (10,20). Budget $2400 buys four pillboxes. Cluster all four inside the corridor so overlapping fire shreds the column at the choke. Spreading across rows the corridor doesn't reach is a wasted budget. Yard intact, ten kills, within about 60 turns.
WIN WHEN: own ≥4 'pbox' building(s) AND have 4 building(s) near (60,20) AND destroy ≥10 enemy units AND own ≥1 'fact' building(s) AND before game tick 5400.
YOU LOSE IF: (not before game tick 5401 OR NOT (own ≥1 'fact' building(s))).
You have at most 60 decision turns; acting decisively and early matters.

Open arena. The enemy composition flips by seed: either ONE concentrated column on y=20 or FOUR squads spread across y=4/12/28/36 (with per-row decoys at x=4 that keep each spread squad on its own latitude). Read the threat from your observation and pick the topology that matches — cluster the four pillboxes at (60,20) for the concentrated thrust, OR spread one per row at x=60 for the wide front. The wrong topology fails the kill quota. Yard intact, eight kills, within about 70 turns.
WIN WHEN: own ≥4 'pbox' building(s) AND (have 4 building(s) near (60,20) OR have 1 building(s) near (60,4) AND have 1 building(s) near (60,12) AND have 1 building(s) near (60,28) AND have 1 building(s) near (60,36)) AND destroy ≥8 enemy units AND own ≥1 'fact' building(s) AND before game tick 6300.
YOU LOSE IF: (not before game tick 6301 OR NOT (own ≥1 'fact' building(s))).
You have at most 70 decision turns; acting decisively and early matters.

title: Defense Doctrine — Walls vs Towers per Tier

raw.realWorldMeaning: Defensive doctrine selection: the same budget buys different postures. An open frontal arc needs ACTIVE covering fires (pbox pillboxes). A numerically overwhelming horde on one lane needs PASSIVE channelisation (a brik wall barrier) plus a single pbox at the choke to shred the queue. A mixed two-lane attack forces a TRADEOFF: choke one lane, cover the other. A memorised "always-towers" or "always-walls" play fails the tier where its posture is wrong.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Defensive doctrine: an open arc demands covering fires; a single overwhelming axis demands channelisation (obstacle belt + fires at the choke); a mixed threat demands force allocation across postures. The same budget produces wildly different outcomes depending on which doctrine matches the geometry — a general who always builds towers loses the horde lane and one who always builds walls loses the open arc.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: security architecture, passive vs active mitigation, military fortification
raw.author: openra-bench

en:
Eight riflemen charge your yard from the east. Your $2400 buys either four active pillboxes or twelve inert concrete walls. Walls don't shoot — kills come from the pillboxes. Build four pillboxes wrapping the yard so their fire shreds the rush. Yard intact, four kills, within about 60 turns.
WIN WHEN: own ≥4 'pbox' building(s) AND destroy ≥4 enemy units AND own ≥1 'fact' building(s) AND before game tick 5400.
YOU LOSE IF: (not before game tick 5401 OR NOT (own ≥1 'fact' building(s))).
You have at most 60 decision turns; acting decisively and early matters.

A massive horde — sixteen riflemen plus four rocket soldiers — funnels at your yard from the east on a single lane. Your $2400 buys either ~12 inert walls or 4 active pillboxes. Neither alone satisfies the doctrine here: pure walls kill nothing, pure pillboxes leave the horde un-channelised. Build a wall belt that channels the horde to a tight pass, with a pillbox at the choke to shred the queue. Yard intact, ten kills, within about 60 turns.
WIN WHEN: own ≥1 'pbox' building(s) AND own ≥6 'brik' building(s) AND destroy ≥10 enemy units AND own ≥1 'fact' building(s) AND before game tick 5400.
YOU LOSE IF: (not before game tick 5401 OR NOT (own ≥1 'fact' building(s))).
You have at most 60 decision turns; acting decisively and early matters.

Your yard spawns NORTH (y=14) or SOUTH (y=26) by seed. TWO waves arrive — a heavy horde on your yard's lane and another on the opposite lane. Your $3000 buys a tradeoff: channel the horde with a wall belt + pillbox at the choke AND post a flanking pillbox on the opposite lane. Yard intact, ten kills, within about 60 turns.
WIN WHEN: own ≥2 'pbox' building(s) AND own ≥6 'brik' building(s) AND destroy ≥10 enemy units AND own ≥1 'fact' building(s) AND before game tick 5400.
YOU LOSE IF: (not before game tick 5401 OR NOT (own ≥1 'fact' building(s))).
You have at most 60 decision turns; acting decisively and early matters.

title: Defend While Building — Concurrent Defence + Construction Under Active Attack

raw.realWorldMeaning: While the enemy is already attacking your base, you must build new pillboxes AND command your pre-placed (HoldFire) tank defenders to attack the rush — IN PARALLEL, every turn. The tanks will NOT engage on their own; only an explicit attack_unit / attack_move order makes them fight. Pausing the pillbox queue to micro the tanks loses the production race (the pbox bar is never met before the deadline). Pausing the tank defence to focus on building loses the fact (the idle HoldFire tanks let the rush walk through and raze the construction yard). Only a play that streams both — queue pbox AND command tanks every turn from t=0 — wins inside the budget. The win predicate makes this load-bearing by requiring BOTH the pbox count bar AND the fact-alive bar AND a kill floor, all before a tight deadline.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: SRE simultaneous incident-response + capacity-add: the on-call must contain the live incident (defence) WHILE provisioning additional capacity (construction) to absorb the increased load; serialising the two — pause provisioning to fight the fire, then provision after — busts the MTTR / capacity-SLA window. Same pattern in military business-continuity (combat engineers emplace fortifications under direct fire while line units engage), ops triage during incident (multiple work streams must advance in parallel), and disaster-recovery failover (route traffic to the spare WHILE rebuilding the primary).
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SRE simultaneous incident-response, business continuity, ops triage during incident

title: Fog Ambush — Hold the Hidden Flank, Let the Enemy Walk Past

raw.realWorldMeaning: Defenders are pre-staged in concealment OFF the direct enemy axis, forming an L-ambush crossfire at the lane. A static fixing element at the choke draws the enemy push down the lane; the concealed flanking elements remain hidden until the band commits, then strike from BOTH flanks. Breaking the ambush — charging the flankers forward to meet the push in the open, or pulling them back onto the construction yard — abandons the crossfire geometry: the charging force strings out and is out-attritioned head-on, and the stacked force is crowded against the base and ground down. The canonical answer is to HOLD the ambush positions and let the engine auto-engage on sight as the band passes. SC2 hidden-defense / military ambush doctrine.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Concealed intrusion-detection sensors / honeypot networks / silent-alarm doctrine: instrumented assets remain off the intruder's primary path and trigger when the intruder commits past them. Moving the sensors out of their concealed positions — forward to confront the intruder, or back onto the asset being protected — defeats the asymmetry of concealment.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 hidden defense, military ambush doctrine, fog warfare
raw.author: openra-bench

title: Hold the Line — Survive an Opening Rush While Sustaining Throughput

raw.realWorldMeaning: Opening rush-defense while sustaining baseline economy growth: a concentrated enemy charge arrives in the first ~30 turns and a pre-placed base + a fixed budget must both blunt the spike AND keep fielding capability. Cannot pause throughput (the win demands an active force) AND cannot ignore the threat (the win demands the rushers handled before the deadline) — both must be sustained simultaneously inside a tight window. Stalling, all-defense (only static turrets, no force), all-economy (no static defense), and brute-army (no static defense) all fail; the intended balanced spend — one pillbox covering the lane mouth plus a handful of defenders trained from the pre-placed barracks — wins.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: On-call defending production capacity under a live attack without dropping baseline SLA: a single concentrated incident hits a pre-deployed site (factory floor / web tier), and the operator must both contain the spike (add a hardened defence at the choke) AND keep the line running (deploy active workers / pods) before the incident clock expires. Pausing throughput to fight, or fighting without hardening, both bust the SLA.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: MicroRTS rush-defense, SC2LE defend-the-cheese tempo, TextStarCraft II opening defense, incident response: production infra under DDoS while sustaining throughput
raw.author: openra-bench

title: Burn-Rate Management — Spend at the Right Pace (Startup Runway)

raw.realWorldMeaning: A sustained cash-rate decision: the agent has a productive income engine (two harvesters on two near patches feeding a refinery — steady ~190 cr/turn), a starting balance of $1500, a war factory + barracks for converting cash into military force, 3 pre-placed medium tanks ready to engage, and a pre-placed enemy garrison to defeat. Winning REQUIRES landing cash in a target BAND [MIN, MAX] at the latch tick AND racking up K kills AND keeping the construction yard intact. Stalling or pure-hoarding pushes cash ABOVE the upper bound (the bank overflows, no progress on the combat bar). Burning every credit on units and buildings drops cash BELOW the lower bound (no reserve, no slack against the next shock). Only a SUSTAINED burn at the income-replenishment rate — converting cash to a small but sufficient combat force while using the existing strike force to clear the garrison — hits the band on the kill-bar turn.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Operating-rate management in a startup's treasury: burn cash on capability development at the rate that buys ongoing runway, not zero (no capability progress — the deadline arrives with no product) and not all-at-once (the reserve hits zero and the next shock — a key hire, an unexpected legal cost — collapses the company). The discipline being measured is the operations-finance LOOP at sustained pace, not a one-time allocation. The cash band is the operating-reserve discipline; the kill bar is the capability-delivery discipline; the two must be satisfied SIMULTANEOUSLY at the deadline.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: startup runway management, corporate burn rate, financial discipline, SC2 mineral-bank overflow (spend down at sustained rate), operating-rate / cash-conversion-rate discipline

title: Capex vs Opex Under Rush Pressure — Buy 4 Tanks NOW or Build a Second Factory?

raw.realWorldMeaning: A fixed cash budget funds EITHER an immediate force (buy 4× medium tanks RIGHT NOW from the pre-placed war factory) OR a long-run capacity upgrade (build a SECOND war factory to double per-turn tank production). A rusher band is incoming at the lane mouth from turn 0 and charges the agent's construction yard. The intended play reads the threat timing and commits the budget to immediate units; spending it on capacity instead leaves no force for the rush, and the construction yard is razed before the new factory fields a single tank. The pack frames the classic CAPEX-vs-OPEX decision: invest for tomorrow vs operate for today.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Operational capacity allocation under a live incident: the budget funds either an immediate dispatch of available robots (OPEX — use existing fleet capacity right now to handle the incident) or procurement of a second loading dock that will double dispatch throughput over the next quarter (CAPEX — long-run capacity). An in-progress incident makes the CAPEX play wrong: spending on the second loading dock now leaves the site undefended, and the incident escalates before the new capacity comes online.

title: Economy — Cash Reserve Management (Spend Without Going Broke)

raw.realWorldMeaning:
A treasury-management decision under a deadline. The agent has a productive operation (two harvesters on two near patches feeding a refinery — steady income), starting cash 1500, and a hard win requirement to grow operations (build MORE buildings) WHILE also finishing the episode with a positive operating reserve in the bank (cash ≥ 300). The classic anti-patterns: 1) STALL — preserve every credit, build nothing. The reserve stays
   safe but operations never grow → the "build more buildings" bar
   is never met → LOSS.
2) OVER-SPEND — spend everything (and then some, by chaining a
   1400cr refinery and any other expensive build) on construction
   and dip the reserve to zero. Income eventually refills but the
   window between buildings-met and reserve-refilled may not close
   before the deadline → LOSS.
3) PURE-HOLD — harvest and sit on the cash forever, never building.
   Same as STALL on the building-growth axis → LOSS.
The intended capability is the SC2 cash-overflow / corporate treasury discipline: spend ENOUGH to keep growing (buildings) while keeping ENOUGH liquid (cash) to weather the next shock — never let the operating reserve hit zero, never sit on idle capital. With a pre-placed 2× harv income engine the model gets ~190 cr/turn of inflow, so any modest spend (1-2 powr at 300cr each) is recovered in a handful of turns and the reserve closes the episode well above 300.

A pure-hoarding policy fails the growth mandate; a blow-the-reserve policy succumbs to the next shock. The discipline being measured is the operations-finance loop: spend at the income-replenishment rate, not above and not below.

title: Contested Central Ore Patch — Common-Pool Resource vs Enemy Raider

raw.realWorldMeaning: Common-pool resource contention with an active rival. A shared ore patch sits in the middle of the map; the enemy fields its own harvesters AND a worker-priority raider bot that drives specifically at your harvesters. Pure extraction (mine only, don't defend) lets the raider pick off your harvs at the contested patch; pure defense (engage the raider, but stop mining) abandons the revenue stream; stalling commits to neither and the economy clock bites. The intended committed-balance play keeps the pre-ringed defenders on station (auto-engaging the inbound raider) AND keeps every harvester in `harvest` mode each turn — extracting THROUGH the contestation, not after it.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Multi-agent extraction from a shared resource zone with an actively-hostile rival fleet. The harvesters keep visiting the contested deposit; the defender fleet must intercept the rival's worker-priority raiders BEFORE they reach the collectors, without leaving the patch unmanned. Abandoning either function — extraction or interception — loses the day to a one-sided commit.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 contested mining / split-base play, game theory common-pool resource (Hardin tragedy of commons), competitive market entry / TAM contention, fishing common-resource dynamics

title: Econ Contested Expansion — Second Refinery on the Contested Patch

raw.realWorldMeaning: Mid-game expansion under genuine geographic contention. The agent owns a working mini-base in one corner of the map and a pair of starter tanks. A richer ore patch sits midway across the map, framed by terrain (water walls) that funnel both sides into a single approach corridor. Enemy patrol infantry already loiter on the patch. The capability under test is to read the tactical position (single approach lane, contested by light infantry that will murder an unarmed harvester), commit the 1400-credit refinery, place it ON the patch (so the engine's free auto-harvester spawns on-site and mines the rich patch via the closest-by-path refinery), and escort with the starter tanks so the patrol doesn't deny the expansion. Stalling, planting the 2nd refinery at home, and committing the refinery without escorting all LOSE.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Commit a forward processor to a contested deposit, with convoy security. An autonomous extraction operation is mining a small home deposit at sub-quota throughput; a richer deposit sits across a contested corridor, patrolled by hostile platforms. The forward processor commission ships with a co-deployed extractor on-site, but the extractor is unarmed and the patrol will destroy it within seconds unless the operator dispatches the available defensive platforms ahead of the commission. Stalling at the home throughput rate never clears the daily revenue target; commissioning the processor at home doubles processors but doesn't add a new deposit; commissioning the processor on the contested deposit without convoy security loses the extractor on first contact.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 contested expansion (take a 2nd resource under harass), facility-siting under adversarial contention, convoy security: forward asset commission + escort, RTS second-refinery idiom (free-worker on-build, at the new proc)

title: Reasoning — Deny the Enemy Expansion (Raid the Contested Refinery)

raw.realWorldMeaning: The enemy has just taken a SECOND base — a refinery (proc) and a harvester (harv) at a contested ore patch in the middle of the map — and it is still only lightly defended. The enemy's MAIN base is far to the east, heavily fortified. Turtling at home lets the enemy economy snowball uncontested; throwing the army at the fortified main just gets it shredded. The winning play is the economic raid: drive the four-tank strike force out to the mid-map expansion, raze the refinery before the deadline to deny the enemy its economic upside, and bring ≥2 tanks home with your construction yard intact. The decision under test is recognising that a soft, freshly-placed enemy expansion is the highest-value target on the board — punish it now, do not turtle and do not over-commit into the fortified main.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Adversarial resource interdiction: an agent must identify that the opponent's newest, least-defended supply node is the decisive target and dispatch a strike to neutralise it within a deadline — rather than passively defending its own assets while the opponent's resource base compounds, or wastefully assaulting the opponent's hardened core.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 expansion denial, economic warfare, resource interdiction

title: Econ — Add the 2nd Harvester Before Break-Even

raw.realWorldMeaning: Capacity-expansion timing under a hard deadline. A revenue operation is running below the throughput it needs to clear a stated target by a stated date; the supervisor holds exactly enough budget for ONE more collector. A collector costs cash up front and has a warmup before it returns revenue, so its payback period only fits inside the planning horizon if the capex is committed EARLY. The decision is the timing: recognise that current capacity misses the bar, and add the second collector before the break-even tick — not "expand eventually". Stalling, running the single collector, buying the collector too late, or spending the reserve on a non-revenue line all miss the target.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Throughput scaling in an autonomous collection fleet: a target output must be met by a hard deadline; one extra collector can be afforded; the collector has acquisition cost plus a spin-up delay before it is productive. Add it early and its payback period fits the horizon and the target clears; add it late and the extra throughput does not run long enough — the deadline passes short. Break-even timing of a capacity capex is the test.

title: Economy — Far Large Patch vs Near Small Patch (Travel-vs-Throughput)

raw.realWorldMeaning: Travel-vs-throughput patch selection under a hard economy deadline. The agent owns ONE harvester, a refinery and a construction yard, and faces TWO ore patches: a NEAR patch a short hop from the refinery, and a FAR patch much farther out. The two patches are NOT symmetric — the near one is small (less total ore) and the far one is large (more total ore) — so the naive "bigger pile is better" heuristic points at the far patch. But the win predicate sets a CASH BAR that must be cleared inside a TIGHT tick deadline, and that deadline is the discriminator: the near patch's short round-trip lets the harvester complete many delivery cycles and bank the bar comfortably before the clock runs out, while the far patch's long round-trip burns so much travel time per cycle that the harvester cannot bank the bar in time NO MATTER how large the far pile is — its greater total is irrelevant inside this window. Mining the far patch busts the clock and LOSES; stalling earns zero and LOSES; the intended capability is the OR travel-vs-throughput / SC2 expansion-timing insight — under a tight deadline, round-trip latency dominates pile size, so route to the near source.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Pickup-station selection under a delivery deadline: a single autonomous hauler, a depot, and two supply nodes — a small nearby node and a large distant node. With an SLA deadline on cumulative delivered volume, the optimal policy routes to the NEAR node because cycle latency (travel time per round trip), not node capacity, bounds throughput inside the window; the distant node's larger stockpile only pays off on a longer horizon. Choosing the big-but-distant node misses the SLA.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: OR travel-vs-throughput, SC2 expansion timing, logistics routing

title: Econ Harvester Defense — Keep the Harv Alive Under Raid Waves

raw.realWorldMeaning: A live extraction operation under recurring asset-targeted harass. The agent owns a refinery, a single harvester running an auto-harvest loop on a nearby ore patch, and a small escort parked at the depot on hold-fire. The harvester's income is the sole revenue stream, and a recurring raider drives at the harvester specifically (not the base, not the escort). The decision is to FLIP the escort from passive to active — set its stance to defend / attack-anything, or order it onto the harvester's lane to intercept — so the raider dies on the escort's fire envelope before reaching the harvester. The map geometry funnels every raider through a single corridor mouth, so the right place to plant the escort is unambiguous if the agent reads the map. Stalling, leaving the escort on hold-fire, or spreading defense everywhere instead of on the corridor mouth all let the harvester die.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Mining-fleet protection under recurring asset-targeted attack — an autonomous extraction site with an extractor robot, a processing depot, and a static defense detail. If the defense detail is in safe-mode (hold fire) the recurring attacker destroys the extractor on the first cycle; the operator must flip the detail to engage and reposition it onto the single access route the attacker must use.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 harvester harass defense (Lambo, Reaper drops on workers), convoy / extractor protection under recurring harass, RTS stance management — flip escort from passive to active, SOC active-vs-passive monitoring posture, chokepoint defense — plant the line on the one route

en:
You own a Construction Yard, Power Plant, Refinery (NW corner, around y=10..12), ONE Ore Truck on auto-harvest to an OFF-AXIS ore patch SOUTH of base at (30,28), and TWO medium tanks (2tnk) parked at your refinery on HOLD-FIRE stance. A vertical water wall at x=46..54 splits the map; the ONLY crossing is a 4-cell corridor at y=18..21. At tick 600 an enemy raider tank spawns at (75,20) in the eastern lobe and drives at your harvester — it MUST come through the corridor to reach you. Win when cash >= 1200 AND your harvester is still alive AND your refinery is intact, before tick 3000. Standing the escort idle (HOLD-FIRE) at base lets the raider walk through and kill the harvester. The intended play is to FLIP the escort's stance to Defend (2) or AttackAnything (3) AND move it onto the west corridor mouth (around x=44..46, y=18..21) so the raider dies on its way out of the corridor.
WIN WHEN: in this exact order: not before game tick 1700 → THEN → hold ≥1200 credits AND have ≥1 'harv' AND own a 'proc' AND before game tick 3000.
YOU LOSE IF: (not before game tick 3001 OR NOT (have ≥1 'harv') OR NOT (own a 'proc')).
You have at most 35 decision turns; acting decisively and early matters.

title: Economy — Harvester Pathing Optimization (Split-Routing M/M/c)

raw.realWorldMeaning: Split-routing under heterogeneous round-trip cost. The agent owns TWO harvesters and faces TWO ore patches: A — a NEAR small patch (rich per-cell but quickly exhausted by two collectors stacking on it) — and B — a FAR larger patch (slow per-cycle but doesn't saturate). The optimal policy sends ONE harvester to A and ONE to B (the "split route"), so the proc receives a steady alternating delivery stream from two short and one long round-trip cycle. The LAZY/BRUTE alternatives both fail: piling BOTH harvs on A pumps early cash but never enters B's region (the routing constraint in the win predicate goes unmet); piling BOTH on B earns barely any income within the deadline (long round-trip dominates). Stalling earns zero. The capability under test is the OR vehicle-routing / SC2 worker-distribution insight: distribute collectors across heterogeneous sources to balance round-trip throughput, not to monocrop the best-looking node.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Fleet vehicle-routing across a multi-server queueing system (M/M/c): two pickup stations at different distances from a depot, each modelled as a server with its own service rate; the optimal fleet allocation puts exactly one vehicle per server so the depot queue alternates arrivals from heterogeneous cycle times rather than stacking all vehicles on the lowest-latency server (which saturates the server and starves throughput) or the highest-throughput server (which dominates the cycle and starves the depot in early windows).
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 worker distribution, OR vehicle routing, M/M/c queueing
raw.author: wave7-fleet

title: Econ Mine and Grow — Place the Refinery on the Ore Patch

raw.realWorldMeaning: Geographic placement of a processing facility relative to the raw resource. The agent owns a Construction Yard, a power plant, and an idle Ore Truck; ONE ore patch is visible on the map. The decision is where to drop the refinery — adjacent to the patch yields short round-trips and steady income; far from the patch starves throughput; not placing it at all leaves the harvester idle. The capability is reading the ore-cells map channel and siting infrastructure near the demand point.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Drop a processing depot at the well-head. An autonomous extraction operation arrives at a site with a collector vehicle and a budget for one processing module. Placing the module beside the resource yields cycle-time-bounded throughput; placing it across the facility yields throughput dominated by transit time; not placing it leaves the collector idle. The mission deadline is real.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2LE CollectMineralsAndGas (placement variant), facility-siting near a raw-resource node, RTS first-refinery-on-the-patch idiom

title: Multi-Patch Allocation — Pick Which Ore Patches To Commit To

raw.realWorldMeaning: Resource allocation across multiple candidate sites under a hard capital budget. The agent has a Construction Yard and a Power Plant in the west and looks out at four ore patches scattered around the map, each with an idle Ore Truck waiting beside it: one small near patch (depletes fast), two medium patches at the medium-distance ring, and one rich patch at the far east edge. Starting cash funds ONE refinery up front; the second requires deposits from the first. The decision is whether to commit to at least two refineries (the multi-patch allocation insight), and which patches to commit them to — stalling earns nothing and loses, a single-refinery opening fails the proc-count clause, and the intended efficient play is to commit to two medium-distance patches so parallel harvest cycles deposit ample cash inside the deadline.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: A mining survey reports four candidate extraction sites with different size and travel-cost profiles, and the day's CAPEX budget covers no more than two processing depots up front. The autonomous operations planner must (a) commit to building more than one processing depot — running only one stalls the quota — and (b) site them next to patches whose harvester cycle-times stay short enough to deposit the quota before the shift deadline. The capability under test is the multi-site-investment decision under a small CAPEX cap, not a single-site optimisation.

title: Overflow To Silos — Build Storage Or Income Spoils At The Cap

raw.realWorldMeaning: Capacity planning under high producer throughput. The agent owns a minimum revenue kit (fact + proc + powr + many harvs on a dense ore patch column) whose harvesters deposit ore at a sustained rate exceeding the refinery's 2000-ore storage cap. Once the cap saturates, every new deposit is LOST — the back-pressure footgun. The decision is to recognise the throughput-vs-buffer gap and BUILD SILOS (cost 150, +3000 cap each) so the working capital is absorbed and the economy_value bar lands INSIDE the within_ticks budget. A run with no silo cannot reach the bar in time (overflow-bound accrual is too slow against the tight deadline); intended capacity-planning runs (build 1-3 silos) WIN.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Distributed-systems back-pressure / FIFO perishable inventory cap. A producer pipeline (sensor capture, log shipping, the data plane) generates events at a sustained rate; the consumer's buffer (the queue, the warehouse, the refinery store) has a fixed cap; when the buffer fills, new events are silently dropped on deposit. The operator must size the buffer (add silos / scale the queue / add warehouse storage) to match producer throughput, or the income channel runs at the buffer's drain rate forever. This pack tests the capacity-planning reflex — measure throughput, measure cap, size the buffer above throughput.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: capacity planning, distributed-systems backpressure, FIFO inventory

title: Protect the Harvester Route — Intercept Raiders on the Supply Line

raw.realWorldMeaning: Defend a long-distance supply line by intercepting the threat ON the route, not at the depot. A single harvester commutes far between refinery and ore patch; a worker-priority raider drives at it from the far end. Defenders pre-placed at the base have no line of sight to the mid-route kill zone — they must be moved out along the harvester's commute axis to intercept the raider before it reaches the harvester. Stalling or holding defenders at base lets the raider kill the harvester on the road; the income bar is unmet; the run loses.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Convoy / supply-line protection on the road. The protective detail rides WITH the convoy along the route, not at the warehouse: a threat that enters the route's mid-span and the escorts that stayed at the depot are out of contact and out of position. The supply line is only safe if patrolled along its full length.

title: Quantity vs Quality — Pick the Right Composition for the Budget

raw.realWorldMeaning: A fixed cash budget funds either a SWARM of cheap rifle infantry (8× e1 @ $100) OR a small ELITE armoured fist (3× 3tnk @ $950). Either composition fits the same budget — the decision is which is right for the threat the agent must clear. The kill bar AND the attrition cap jointly bind: a stall never reaches the bar; a mixed mini-spend (1 tank + a handful of rifles) underdelivers on DPS and bleeds units past the loss cap; one of the two pure compositions cleanly wins per tier. Hard flips the right answer per seed — the agent's spawn corner determines which garrison is local, and the local garrison's composition determines whether mass cheap or few elite is the right counter (anti-vehicle garrison ⇒ mass cheap wins, anti-infantry garrison ⇒ elite armour wins).
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Fleet provisioning under a fixed CAPEX: same budget buys either a swarm of cheap general-purpose drones or a handful of expensive high-capability robots. The mission profile (debris field vs high-value point target; mass surveillance vs precision strike) decides which composition is right — and a half-and-half procurement satisfies neither requirement.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 mass-vs-elite army composition, industrial mass-production vs craftsmanship, military doctrine: quantity has a quality of its own, OR unit-composition optimization under budget

title: Recover From Zero Cash — Rebuild Revenue From a Minimum-Viable Kit

raw.realWorldMeaning: Turtle-recovery / bankruptcy turnaround from a minimum-viable kit and zero working capital. The agent inherits ONE refinery, ONE harvester, and ONE ore patch — but no cash, no spare workers, no army. The decision is the RECOVERY PROFILE — commit to harvest FIRST (the only income channel), accumulate cash, and then reinvest in the NEXT productive asset (a war factory and a second harvester) so the income channel actually scales past a non-trivial revenue bar before the deadline. Stalling (no income), spending the accumulated cash on the wrong asset (a second refinery, army units), or trying to build an army from zero all miss the bar.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Post-crisis operations restart: an autonomous operator has lost most of its infrastructure and is reduced to one processing unit, one collector, and one known source — with no operating capital. It must commit to running the collector to refill the cash reserve, then deploy the saved capital to acquire a second collector before the recovery deadline. Spending on defensive / expansion hedges before the income channel has refilled the reserve misses the bar.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 turtle-back-to-economy / recovery from setback, business bankruptcy turnaround planning, military recovery from defeat (rebuild force structure), startup pivot after runway crisis
raw.author: groupF-econ-seed

title: Replace Dead Harvester — Replan Economy After Exogenous Loss

raw.realWorldMeaning: Reactive replan after an exogenous worker death. A productive operation suddenly loses a value-generating unit to an outside event; cash reserves are tuned for EXACTLY one replacement; the deadline is real. The agent must notice the loss, commit the reserve to rebuilding the dead worker (not to army units), and redirect production back to the same revenue loop — fast enough that the deadline still bites.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Pipeline / fleet operation where one autonomous collector is destroyed mid-mission by an external hazard. The remaining collectors stay in the loop; the supervisor has just enough budget for a single replacement; redirecting the new unit back to the same revenue source AND re-tasking the survivors (whose loop was interrupted by the loss event) is the test. Spending the reserve on defenders, or stalling, misses the throughput bar.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: PlanBench replanning under exogenous loss, ScienceWorld error recovery, SC2 replace-killed-workers reflex, disaster recovery: worker replacement
raw.author: openra-bench

title: Resource Trade With Self — Hedge The Stockpile-vs-Cash Balance

raw.realWorldMeaning: The agent runs a high-throughput economy (fact + proc + powr + 7 harvesters on a dense ore patch) and every tick "trades with itself": harvested ore either sits as STOCKPILE in the refinery store or converts to CASH through a rate-limited drain. The two forms count equally toward book value (economy_value = cash + stored ore), but the stockpile side is CAP-LIMITED — once the 2000-ore refinery store fills, every new deposit is LOST. The decision is how much storage to buy: building silos (cost 150, +3000 cap each) lifts the cap so income is never spoiled, but each silo is 150 cash off the book and one build-queue turn. Build too FEW silos and the cap floods and discards income; build too MANY and the cash sunk into idle storage plus the queue turns drag book value below the target. The winning play is the hedged middle — size the buffer to the throughput, neither under nor over.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Commodity hedging / finance inventory-vs-cash balance. A producer of a physical commodity decides each period how much output to BANK as inventory versus SELL into cash. Inventory carries a cost (storage capex, here the silo spend and the build-queue turns) and a finite warehouse cap (overflow past the cap is product lost); cash is liquid but the conversion channel is rate-limited. The value-maximising position is the hedge: size the warehouse to absorb production — under-buffering spoils output, over-buffering sinks capital into idle storage. This pack tests the two-sided balancing reflex: measure throughput, measure cap, buy exactly enough buffer.

title: Econ Second-Base Race — Plant the 2nd Proc at the Contested Spot

raw.realWorldMeaning: Tempo expansion to a SPECIFIC second-base location under a hard deadline. The agent owns a Construction Yard, a Power Plant, an idle Ore Truck, and a small near-base ore patch in the NORTH- WEST corner of a medium arena. A rich CONTESTED ore patch sits far to the south-east — the only zone where a 2nd refinery produces enough income to clear the cash bar inside the clock. The capability under test is the TEMPO + SPATIAL decision to drop the 2nd `proc` inside the contested target disk (radius 6 around the patch) on turn 1, rather than placing it at home (the comfortable adjacency-to-fact play) or anywhere on the map that is not the target spot. A home-placed `proc` still runs an economy off the near-base patch — but the cash bar is not the only gate: the `building_in_region` clause requires the proc to be at the target zone, so a home play loses on the spatial predicate even with the bar cleared.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Forward-deploy a processing module at a SPECIFIC contested extraction site under a hard deadline. The home depot has a small local deposit (sustaining income but well below quota); the only way to hit the throughput SLA is to commit the second module to the far site, accepting that you cannot recover it if you mis-spend. The decision is geographic commitment to a specific cell, not a directional gradient — placing the module "somewhere forward" but missing the cell fails the placement audit.

title: Silo vs Spend — Storage-Cap Working-Capital Allocation

raw.realWorldMeaning: Capital-allocation under a perishable storage cap. The agent runs a revenue kit (fact + proc + powr + harv on an ore patch) whose income flows into a CAPPED storage pool (the refinery store): once full, new harvested ore is lost on deposit. The decision every turn is what to do with the working capital that's accumulating: either SPEND it on productive combat assets (build infantry, kill the enemy garrison), SPEND it on fixed defensive assets (build a pbox line), OR BUILD A SILO so the storage cap grows and ore keeps banking. All three paths legitimately resolve the cap pressure; the only failure mode is HOARDING — observing without building or killing, which leaves capacity to spoil and never satisfies the "use the capital" mandate (the any_of clause).
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Working-capital management for a robotic operations stack with a FIFO inventory cap: a collector pipeline deposits perishable goods into a fixed-capacity warehouse, and a continuous spend channel converts warehouse stock into bank capital. The operator must EITHER deploy the bank capital on productive assets (extra collectors, defenders), build fixed infrastructure (fortified pickets), OR expand the warehouse (build storage so each new collection still has somewhere to go). Letting capital sit idle while the warehouse fills loses goods at the cap — the perishable-inventory / cash-conversion-cycle discipline.

title: Econ Startup From Scratch — Greenfield First Base From Zero

raw.realWorldMeaning: Greenfield first-base economy ramp from zero infrastructure: the agent begins with one mobile asset (the MCV) and a cash budget but NO buildings, NO harvesters, and NO income. The opening decision is the entire test — deploy the MCV (irreversibly converting it to a Construction Yard), then stand up the first power plant (prerequisite) and the first ore refinery (which auto-spawns a free harvester), and finally commit to harvesting so the income pipeline actually closes the revenue gap before the clock. A model that stalls, that spends the budget on infantry / military buildings, or that deploys and then idles, all miss the revenue bar and the clock runs out as a real loss.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Cold-start a revenue pipeline: an autonomous operator arrives at a greenfield site with capital and a single mobile depot. title: Econ — Hit a Cash Target by a Hard Deadline

raw.realWorldMeaning: Budget-by-date target: the operation must reach a stated cash bar by a stated deadline, the way a startup must hit a quarterly revenue target / a fundraising milestone / a quarterly closeout. Pre-placed harvester+refinery+barracks are the running pipeline; the agent must reason about whether the current capacity will clear the bar on time, and if not, reinvest into harvesting capacity (build extra harvesters) — not into army units that drain the cash account without growing income. Idling, over-spending on the wrong line item, or under-investing in capacity all miss the bar.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Throughput-by-deadline planning in an autonomous pipeline: hit a revenue/output target by a hard date by deciding when to scale up collectors (capacity capex) vs hold (stay lean) vs spend on unrelated capacity (army units / non-revenue line items). Capex timing is the decision — over-spend on the wrong line and the deadline passes with the books short.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 econ-by-tick target, budget-by-date / quarterly revenue target, fundraising milestone planning, OR throughput optimization with deadline

title: Capital Allocation — Tech Building or Economic Expansion?

raw.realWorldMeaning: One indivisible budget funds EITHER a tech building (a war factory — a capability investment that generates no income) OR an economic expansion (a second ore harvester that roughly doubles gathering throughput). The regime is fixed: there is no near-term combat demand the tech tier must satisfy, so the budget compounds best as capacity. The win is an economy target by a deadline — expanding clears it; sinking the budget into the non-revenue tech building leaves the economy short. The pack frames the classic tech-vs-expand decision: do not buy capability the regime does not yet demand when the same budget, spent on capacity, compounds.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Capital budgeting for an autonomous operation: the same budget buys EITHER a new capability module that the current mission profile does not call for OR an extra collector that compounds throughput over the planning horizon. With no demand the new capability serves inside the horizon, the capacity expansion dominates on payback — invest in throughput, not in idle capability.

title: Harvest Economy — Capital Reinvestment (Wide vs Deep vs Geographic)

raw.realWorldMeaning: Early-revenue capital reinvestment under a deadline. A productive operation has just enough starting capital for ONE coherent capacity expansion: deepen the team at the near patch (extra harvester), widen processing (extra refinery), or expand geographically (send a new harvester to a far patch). Hedging (splitting the indivisible budget across two reinvestments) funds neither path completely and yields baseline throughput — the deadline bites. The test is committing the whole budget to ONE reinvestment path early, not dithering.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Capacity-expansion budgeting in an autonomous pipeline operation: add a collector (deep), add a processing/staging node (wide), or deploy a collector to an unexploited zone (geographic). The same indivisible budget buys exactly one; a hedged spend yields neither and the mission deadline is missed.

title: Capital Allocation — Commit One Indivisible Budget to a Single Path

raw.realWorldMeaning: A capital-allocation decision under a single indivisible budget that is razor-tight: the cash buys EXACTLY ONE coherent path — a WIDE economy (a second refinery plus supporting power: added depot/throughput capacity) OR a DEEP one (keep the single refinery and convert the whole budget into a larger forward force: collection/utilisation). The budget cannot fund both, and any credit diverted to the other path starves the required one so it never completes in time. The test is committing to and finishing the one correct allocation; a split (hedged) budget builds neither and loses.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Fleet capital allocation under a hard, indivisible budget: the same funds buy EITHER added depot/processing capacity OR added collector/worker agents — the classic throughput-versus-collection trade in an autonomous foraging fleet, where a hedged (split) budget yields neither and the mission deadline is missed.

The budget cannot fund both, and any credit diverted to the other path starves the required one so it never completes in time. The test is committing to and finishing the one correct allocation; a split (hedged) budget builds neither and loses.

en:
Your budget is exactly the cost of a second refinery ($1400) plus its supporting power plant ($300) — $1700 total. Build and place both. Any credit spent on units leaves too little to finish both structures in time. Two refineries, two power plants, within about 22 turns.
WIN WHEN: own ≥2 'proc' building(s) AND own ≥2 'powr' building(s) AND before game tick 1893.
YOU LOSE IF: not before game tick 1893.
You have at most 24 decision turns; acting decisively and early matters.

Same wide-expansion budget plus three infantry ($1700 + $300 = $2000). Build the second refinery, second power plant, AND train three rifles. A fourth unit or any diversion overspends and the second refinery never completes. Three units alive, within about 24 turns.
WIN WHEN: own ≥2 'proc' building(s) AND own ≥2 'powr' building(s) AND keep ≥3 units alive AND before game tick 2073.
YOU LOSE IF: not before game tick 2073.
You have at most 26 decision turns; acting decisively and early matters.

WIN WHEN: keep ≥22 units alive AND own ≥1 'proc' building(s) AND before game tick 2613.
YOU LOSE IF: not before game tick 2613.
You have at most 32 decision turns; acting decisively and early matters.

title: Expansion AGGRO — Rush to 3 Bases (Growth Supremacy, No Defence)

raw.realWorldMeaning: AGGRO triple-expansion: three indivisible base-builders are committed simultaneously to three DISTINCT geographies, with no surviving home base and no army held in reserve. The decision is whether to embrace the greedy growth play (race the clock; bet that no one punishes the open flank in time) or hedge by keeping one MCV back as defence (and forfeit the third region). The enemy in this scenario is intentionally too weak to punish a fully-greedy commit inside the budget — the discrimination is whether the model RECOGNISES that and commits, instead of defaulting to a "safe" partial expansion that fails the bar.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Autonomous fleet land-grab: three indivisible deployable platforms must each anchor at a distinct claim site before a deadline; the fleet has no escort and no fallback, and the only safe play is speed — any platform held back as a "rover reserve" leaves a claim uncontested and forfeits the multi-site network. Same idea in aggressive market-entry (claim three regional markets ahead of competitors) and in blitzscale (deploy capacity faster than rivals can react, accept the unit-economics hit).
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 greedy 3-base macro / fastest expansion timing, startup blitzscale: skip margin for growth, aggressive market-share land-grab, growth-vs-defence tradeoff

title: Expansion BALANCED — 2 Bases, Defend BOTH (Growth + Retention)

raw.realWorldMeaning: BALANCED 2-base expansion: the agent must EXPAND to a second geographic site AND retain the original — the classic growth-with-quality decision. A greedy expander who opens both sites but defends neither loses the original to attrition; a turtle who fortifies the original site but never expands fails the multi-site bar. Only a play that splits investment between new-market entry AND retention infrastructure passes both halves of the brief. The discrimination is whether the model RECOGNISES that the standard balanced macro (expand AND defend) is the bar, not the AGGRO blitzscale (expand only) nor the TURTLE single-site fortress (defend only).
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Autonomous fleet establishing a second forward operating base while keeping a defensive ring around the original: the spare base-builder unit drives to the briefed expansion zone AND the fleet allocates a defensive turret + a small infantry escort at BOTH the new AND the existing base. Skipping either side of the investment loses one site to attrition / a probing intruder before the multi-site network goes live.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 standard 2-base macro / safe-expand timing, sustainable growth: expand AND defend, product expansion-with-quality: new market + retention, balanced macro: growth+defense

title: Expansion TURTLE — Fortify 1 Base (Defence Supremacy, No Expansion)

raw.realWorldMeaning: TURTLE 1-base fortification: the agent has no second MCV and no `deploy` tool — expansion is structurally off the menu. The only path to win is to take the single pre-placed base and harden it so densely (≥6 pillboxes + ≥2 gun turrets + a minimum army of 3) that an incoming hunt-bot assault is absorbed at the wall, with the home fact still standing at the deadline. The discrimination is whether the model embraces the deep-defence play (accepts the 1-base cap and invests the whole economy in static defence + minimum army) instead of defaulting to a "balanced" play that leaves the base under-fortified, or a "pure army" play that gets ground down without towers to anchor on, or an "over-tech" play that builds research while the fact is being razed.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Single-site hardening under known incoming threat: a fixed asset (factory, data centre, military outpost) has a known incoming attack inside a fixed window, no option to relocate, and no reinforcement; the only path is to invest the entire budget in passive hardening (walls, turrets, hardened bunkers) plus a minimum on-site response force, accepting that the asset will be irrelevant outside its own perimeter. Same idea in capital allocation (own one market deeply), cybersecurity (concentrate WAF + IDS + bastion at the one public-facing endpoint instead of spreading thin), and military fortress doctrine (concentrate force at one impregnable site).

title: Harass Response — Engage the Probe, Don't Bleed the Defence

raw.realWorldMeaning: A perimeter alert appears inside live infrastructure (a small probing patrol oscillates onto your refinery). You must pick contain / monitor / hunt without bleeding capacity to the distractor. The intended policy keeps the fire team ON the asset and ORDERS them to engage as the probe swings into range — fire support on home turf. Doing nothing (monitor) lets the probe chip the asset to death; chasing the probe off-map (hunt) overextends the team into the next alt-vector swing and abandons the asset; pulling back (yield / retreat) also abandons the asset. The discrimination is between "respond proportionally on home turf" and three failure modes that all bleed something (the asset, the team, or both).
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Security robot reacting to a probe without leaving the patrol zone unmanned: engage the intruder within the asset's defended footprint; do not pursue past the leash or the parallel sector goes uncovered.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: τ²-bench distractor handling, MineRL react vs pursue wildlife, SOC Tier-2 triage: contain vs monitor vs hunt, perimeter alert response under preservation constraint

title: 100-Turn Marathon Survival — Sustain Defence, Reinforcement, and Repair

raw.realWorldMeaning: A very-late single-episode endurance test: keep the base alive under SUSTAINED enemy pressure for the full 100-turn budget. The win is gated on the base, a minimum garrison, and the pillbox line ALL still being intact at the end of the run, not on a one-shot decision. The intended capability is the cadence of reinforcement (train new infantry every few turns), repair (toggle autorepair on damaged defences), and economic stewardship (keep the refinery's harvester flowing). Stalling, pure defence without reinforcement, and pure construction without repair all lose; only sustained operations survive to the after-ticks gate.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Long-horizon autonomous operation under continuous external pressure: an extended on-call / extended deployment where there is no single decisive action, only the discipline of sustained maintenance — repair work, supply replenishment, force rotation — across the entire window. Credit only arrives at the end of the window if every subsystem is still up.

title: Build Army → Coordinate Multi-Front Attack — Mass-Then-Split

raw.realWorldMeaning: Late-game two-phase operational plan: first ASSEMBLE a real fighting force (≥N medium tanks built from the pre-placed war factory), then COMMIT that force to a simultaneous TWO-FRONT assault on two separated enemy headquarters (NE and SE corners). The `then:` composite enforces the assemble-before-attack ordering and the 120-cell NE↔SE separation enforces the SPLIT — a single mass cannot raze both corners in sequence inside the clock; only build-then-split wins. Sending only the 2 starter units to each front fails (insufficient firepower per prong); stalling fails on the clock; one-front-only fails on the second destruction clause.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Theater-wide operational sequencing: a force must be brought to minimum operational strength BEFORE being committed, and once committed must be split across two simultaneous objectives in different theatres under a single shared deadline. A serialized "clear theatre A then redeploy to B" plan blows the time budget; a "commit understrength to both" plan loses both engagements.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 macro-then-multi-prong-attack, military operational planning (force build then theater assault), PERT theater-wide ops sequencing, industrial product launch: build inventory then multi-region rollout
raw.author: openra-bench

title: Credit Only at the Final Phase — Sparse Reward, One Late Objective

raw.realWorldMeaning: A long-horizon plan where ONLY the terminal outcome is rewarded: raze the far enemy headquarters inside a single late deadline. Building the base, massing the army, marching across the map — none of it scores on its own. The agent must invest early with no feedback, then commit the force on a long trek so the one rewarded event lands in time. Over-investing (building forever, never striking) and under-investing (striking too early with too little) both lose; only correctly-timed commitment toward the distant payoff wins. This is delayed gratification under sparse reward.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: A multi-stage autonomous mission where success is graded solely on completing the final objective by a hard deadline (e.g. a long traverse-then-deliver task): intermediate waypoints and subsystem readiness earn no partial credit, so the planner must allocate the whole time budget toward the single terminal payoff rather than optimising locally-visible sub-progress.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: sparse-reward RL (terminal-only reward, no reward shaping), delayed-gratification / temporal credit assignment, long-horizon credit assignment (terminal-objective payoff), Montezuma's Revenge-style sparse terminal reward
raw.author: berta

title: Econ → Army → Victory — Strict 3-Phase Macro Chain

raw.realWorldMeaning: A long single-episode macro plan whose final win depends on three sequenced milestones: first accumulate enough economy_value (cash + uncashed resources) via harvest income; then assemble a real fighting force (≥6 own units); then commit them to terminal action (≥K enemy kills). The Wave-2 `then:` composite enforces happened-before sequencing — pre-spending all cash on an army before income tops up the M bar cannot complete phase 1, and building economy without ever fielding/attacking with an army cannot complete phases 2-3. Only the intended econ → army → victory chain WINS inside the tick budget.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Long-horizon agentic operation with strict stage gating in an industrial / military context: revenue / fuel / logistics must clear a readiness bar BEFORE a fleet is provisioned, which must be provisioned BEFORE a terminal action (sortie / market entry / mission execution). The credit at episode end requires each stage to have happened, in order, inside one budget window — skipping any stage forfeits the chain.

raw.roboticsAnalogue: Long sequenced operation with strict checkpoint gating: a mission that runs through 5+ phases that must complete in order (sensor coverage → infrastructure → fleet provisioning → contact → objective), inside a single budget window. Standard PERT / CPM critical-path execution where a downstream task cannot start (and cannot earn credit) until its upstream predecessor has finished.

title: Opening → Defense → Counter — Strict 3-Phase Military Chain

raw.realWorldMeaning: A long single-episode military plan whose final win depends on three sequenced milestones: first bring the base online (build the power plant so the pre-placed barracks/refinery come online); then survive a concentrated opening rush (kill enough of the rushers and hold the line past a defence window); then convert the survived defence into an offensive that destroys the enemy construction yard far to the east. The Wave-2 `then:` composite enforces happened-before sequencing — stalling loses the base to the rush, racing the counter first loses the base while undefended, and a pure defence that never counter-attacks cannot complete the chain. Only the intended opening → defense → counter plan WINS inside the tick budget.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Long-horizon agentic operation with strict stage gating in a military / incident-response context: a site must first be brought to operational readiness (power online so the line can run), then survive a concentrated incoming attack (contain the spike and hold past the incident window), then mount the planned response that neutralises the source of the attack. Each stage gates the next inside one budget window — skipping any stage (no readiness, no defence, no response) forfeits the chain.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 timing push, military defense-then-counter, PlanBench long-sequencing, incident response: stabilise then remediate the source

title: Stage-Locked Progression — PERT Critical-Path 5-Stage Chain

raw.realWorldMeaning: A long single-episode operation whose final win depends on FIVE milestones being observed-true in strict order: bring power online (powr), stand up resource intake (proc), accumulate a capital reserve (economy_value ≥ M), unlock the tech tier (weap), then commit to terminal action (≥ K kills). The Wave-2 `then:` composite is a PERT critical path — each milestone node gates its successor, so skipping a stage is impossible by construction: the latch cannot advance past a stage that was never observed true, and the chain never completes. Only the intended ordered progression wins inside the tick budget; any stage-skip or stall forfeits on the clock.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: PERT/CPM critical-path execution of a staged operation: a mission runs through power-up, resource intake, capital/charge reserve, capability unlock and terminal action, and the credit at episode end requires every stage to have happened in sequence inside one budget window. A downstream task cannot start — and cannot earn credit — until its upstream predecessor has finished; an out-of-order or skipped stage forfeits the whole staged plan.

title: Disaster Recovery — Rebuild After a Mid-Game Loss, Still Finish

raw.realWorldMeaning: Reactive replan after a mid-mission exogenous catastrophe wipes part of the operating force and the economy at once. An offensive operation runs on a fixed deadline with a working production base (Construction Yard + Refinery + Power Plant + War Factory + Ore Truck + ore patch) and a forward armoured column. Mid-episode a scheduled disaster — a sabotage strike, a supply-line cut, an industrial accident — destroys the Ore Refinery and two of the forward tanks. The deadline does not move. The model must notice the loss (the live refinery count drops to zero, the tank count falls), commit the reserve to rebuilding the refinery so the income channel is restored, AND press on with the surviving and replacement force to clear the eastern garrison before the original clock expires. Giving up after the loss, rebuilding but never attacking, or attacking but never rebuilding the refinery all miss the bar.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Disaster recovery / PlanBench replanning under an exogenous failure event. An autonomous operation loses a critical infrastructure node and part of its mobile fleet to a single mid-mission catastrophe; the operational objective and timeline are unchanged. Recovery requires recognising the compound loss, committing the reserve to rebuilding the lost infrastructure (not to more mobile units, not to nothing), and continuing the mission with the regenerated force fast enough that the original deadline is still met — the SC2 comeback: rebuild after a bad trade and still hit the timing.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: PlanBench replanning, disaster recovery, SC2 comeback
raw.author: openra-bench-wave-11

title: Scout, React, Counter — Observation-Driven 3-Phase Chain

raw.realWorldMeaning: Reactive macro on a fixed force: the agent must drive the observation-action-counter loop end-to-end inside one budget. Phase 1 (scout) is mandatory — the deeper enemy posture (≥2 buildings worth of structure) must be observed before any commit is informed; phase 2 (react) requires the army to actually engage the cluster, not merely walk past; phase 3 (counter) is the production-yard kill that ends the threat at its source. Pre-committing to attack the construction yard without scouting cannot satisfy the chain — the scout latch is the load-bearing first link.
raw.roboticsAnalogue: Threat-intel-driven incident response: SOC analyst confirms multiple indicators of compromise from telemetry (scout), contains the active attacker on the network (react / engage), then patches the upstream attack vector / takes down the command-and-control host (counter). Skipping the confirmation step and going straight to take-down acts on stale belief and misses the root cause; scouting forever bleeds the response window.
raw.benchmarkAnchor: SC2 reactive macro (scout-pivot-counter), CICERO information-action loop, PlanBench replanning, threat-intel-driven defense
raw.author: openra-bench
